No. 26· 19 November 2026· Global, Italy in focus· Illustrated edition
In three lines

  1. The world

9to5Google, ppc.land · November 12, 2026

Google gives its fastest new AI model to every searcher for free, right as its own data shows search traffic is being eaten by something else

Gemini 4 Hydrogen rolled out globally on November 12 inside Google Search, now the default model behind AI Mode and the model that handles the hardest AI Overviews questions, for everyone, not just subscribers to Google's paid AI plans. Google calls it "the biggest model upgrade to Search yet." The company is splitting its model family by job: Carbon and Argon are built to think deeply, Hydrogen is built to answer fast, and it is Hydrogen that now sits between a billion searches a day and the brands trying to be found in them. The rollout lands two days after SparkToro, the audience-research firm, published new data on where all that attention is actually going: total visits to the world's top 1 million websites fell 12.2% between their first-quarter-2022 peak and the third quarter of 2026, even as the global online population grew roughly 24% over the same stretch, and visits per web user are down 29.2%. The top 10 domains alone grew their share of all that traffic, from 22.5% of the top million's visits in late 2021 to 24.4% now.

Why it mattersGoogle just handed out a faster way to answer questions without ever leaving Google, in the same week independent data confirmed the web outside the walled gardens is shrinking even as more people come online to use it.

The IAB publishes a shared language for AI-assisted sales, because right now nobody agrees on what to call them

The Interactive Advertising Bureau released its AI-Era Attribution Blueprint, a framework that splits every conversion into three buckets: Human-Owned, AI-Assisted, or AI-Executed, and spells out what evidence each claim needs before a brand can credit an AI platform, a search engine, or a human-run campaign for a sale. The blueprint builds on IAB's earlier "Measuring Visibility in the AI Era" playbook and was written by a working group of brand, agency, publisher, AI-platform and measurement leads. The reason it exists: IAB's own 2026 Outlook Study found 45% of ad buyers name comparing AI-driven customer journeys against traditional ones as their single biggest measurement headache, and a separate PPC Land report the same week found only 16% of brands currently track their own AI visibility at all. The IAB is explicit that much of the proof needed to back an AI-attribution claim still sits locked inside the AI platforms themselves, not with the brand or the publisher.

Why it mattersAn industry only writes a measurement standard this detailed once it has already lost the argument about what is actually driving sales, same instinct, new battlefield.
PPC Land, famouscampaigns.com, Scotsman, B&T · November 1 and 12, 2026

System1 publishes its 2026 Christmas ad rankings, and Marks & Spencer manages to prove its own worst week and its own best week inside the same eleven days

On November 1, M&S posted a Christmas graphic of red, green and silver party hats burning in a fireplace that a large share of viewers read as a Palestinian flag; the company apologised and pulled it, and brand sentiment coverage swung sharply both more positive and more negative in the days after (up to 24.7% positive, 20.6% negative, from 18.3% and 12.9% before, per marketing-interactive.com). Eleven days later, System1's early Christmas-ad rankings, published November 12, put M&S's actual TV campaign, "The Home of Christmas," starring a bare-chested James Norton as an undercover Santa (Mother London, directed by Shannon Murphy through Smuggler) in third place with a 5.9-Star Rating, the maximum on System1's scale, tied with Morrisons, Sainsbury's, Aldi, Thatchers, Disney and two others. Eight of the top 12 ads tested hit the maximum 5.9 stars; System1 did not disclose its sample size, test dates, or how many ads it tested in total. One ranking entry closes a thread this brief has carried for two issues: the "Coca-Cola, Holidays Are Coming (AI)" spot in the No. 9 slot (5.7 stars) is not a new 2026 campaign, it traces to Marketing Dive's November 2025 coverage of Coca-Cola's "Refresh Your Holidays" push, itself a reworking of a 2024 spot; Coca-Cola appears to be running the same AI-made ad a second year running rather than building a new one.

Why it mattersThe same brand, the same month, a flat image that read as an atrocity and a moving one that reportedly made people say they "can't stop watching", proof that format and execution carry more risk, and more reward, than the underlying idea ever does.

Social trends

Pinterest Business Community, PBC Weekly Trends Report · November 13, 2026

Pinterest's own weekly dashboard shows search spiking hardest on tiny, specific, slightly absurd things

  • "Starbucks holiday drinks" is up 3,000% week over week on Pinterest, next to a steadier "Winter Style" at +80%.
  • "Disguise a Turkey," the kids' craft where a paper turkey is dressed as something else to dodge Thanksgiving dinner, is up 500%.
  • "Thanksgiving Appetizer Recipes" is up 200%, the only one of the four with an obvious, durable commercial use past this specific week.
Why it mattersThe biggest percentage jumps on Pinterest are almost never the most useful signal for a brand, a 3,000% spike on a tiny base is still a tiny base; the steadier, smaller numbers are usually the ones worth building a campaign around.
B&T · November 2026, citing an October 15 start

A dance trend that started a month ago keeps growing across four countries, no platform dashboard required to see it

  • The "Housewife" trend, built around a specific dance/transition format, has climbed to 313,700 videos since it started on October 15.
  • Creators from the United States, United Kingdom, Germany and the Netherlands are all participating, an unusually wide spread for a single-format trend this deep into its run.
  • No official TikTok view count is available for the trend as a whole; the 313,700 figure counts videos using the associated sound or format, per B&T, not total views.
Why it mattersA month-old trend still adding four-country spread is a trend that has not yet peaked, which is a different, more useful signal than a one-week spike.
Flagged, single-source aggregator (anijam.ai) · November 2026

Instagram Reels rewards structured conflict over polish, according to one aggregator's read of this month's formats, unverified by Meta

The "multi-character debate" format, one creator playing several personas arguing about the same product or situation, is described as one of the fastest-growing Reels structures this month, with jump cuts every 3 to 5 seconds tied to a claimed 32% engagement lift; Reels under 30 seconds in this format are said to post the highest completion rates. None of these figures come from Meta directly or from a named, auditable study; they are reported here as a single aggregator's read of the format's performance, not a platform-confirmed number.

Why it mattersThe format logic, make the internal debate external, is sound and worth testing regardless of whether the specific percentage holds up; the number is the part to distrust, not the idea.

Campaigns & brand moves

ABC30, Laughing Place · short premiered November 9, 2026

Disney skips the product entirely and opens its holiday push with an 8-minute short film about a kid who feels too old for magic

"The Invisible Horse," directed by Dougal Wilson, follows a boy named Jack who thinks he has outgrown the holidays until an invisible creature pulls him back into his own imagination. It anchors "Make the Holidays Magic," a company-wide push spanning Disney+, Hulu, ABC and Freeform, Disney's parks and its cruise line, plus merchandise tied to Avengers, Toy Story and Winnie the Pooh. System1's November 12 rankings (The world, above) gave the short a 5.9-Star Rating, tied for the top score in its Christmas-ad set, despite it never mentioning a single product.

Why it mattersA company that owns this many franchises does not need to sell anything inside the ad; it just needs the feeling to be real enough that the merchandise sells itself afterward.
Mediaweek, Marketing-Interactive · launched November 2, 2026

Woolworths turns 8,000-plus customer food confessions into the actual soundtrack of its Christmas campaign

"Tastes Like Christmas," Woolworths' first campaign with new creative agency Droga5 ANZ, grew out of a social callout asking Australian and New Zealand shoppers what food "tastes like Christmas" to them. More than 8,000 submissions were turned into an original carol, built from customers' own words, that now runs as the spine of the campaign across free-to-air TV, radio, print, out-of-home, YouTube, subscription TV, social and in-store, Woolworths' first trans-Tasman Christmas push. A Spotify partnership adds sponsored, personalised Christmas playlists alongside it.

Why it mattersThe ad's most valuable asset was already sitting in the brand's own comments section; Woolworths just had to be the one to collect it and press play.
Businessonline.it, Dissapore · roadshow November 7-29, 2026

Ferrero builds real scarcity into a biscuit launch, and Italians are already paying triple online before the vans even arrive

Nutella Cookies, Ferrero's second biscuit product built around Nutella after 2019's Nutella Biscuits, reach Italy with only 120,000 packages allotted nationally, roughly 23 tonnes of product, each 196-gram pack holding 7 cookies with a cream filling that makes up 35% of the recipe, developed with Belgian biscuit maker Delacre. A branded van is touring Milan, Turin, Bologna, Rome and Naples from November 7 to 29 with sampling stops. Before the roadshow had properly started, resale listings on Amazon and eBay were already asking roughly double to triple the French retail reference price of 3.49 euros.

Why it mattersFerrero did not need to advertise scarcity, it just had to make the product genuinely scarce; the resale markup is doing the marketing for free.

What is working in content

System1 (data via The world, above)

Supermarkets, mascots and delivery vans still beat spectacle at Christmas, even the AI kind, by System1's own numbers

Look past the single highest score in System1's November 12 rankings and the pattern holds across the whole top 12: Morrisons, Sainsbury's, Aldi and Thatchers all hit the maximum 5.9 stars with ads built on familiar tropes, mascots, a delivery run, a pub landlord, a dog. System1 pairs every Star Rating with a separate "Spike" score, its estimate of short-term sales uplift; the highest Spikes in this set belong to Morrisons and Sainsbury's (1.68 each) and Coca-Cola (1.66), the last one notable because Coca-Cola's entry is not a new ad (The world, above) but a rerun of 2025's AI-generated spot, which still placed ninth on Star Rating, behind seven ads built the traditional way. Novelty, AI-made or otherwise, is not what is winning this category right now; recognisability is.

Why it mattersThe brands spending the most on generative novelty this Christmas are, so far, being outscored by the ones spending on the same mascot they used last year.
Social Media Today · rolled out November 6, 2026

YouTube gives its smallest creators a fan-funded boost button, and Italy is one of the first nine countries to get it

"Hype with Jewels" lets viewers spend Jewels, YouTube's paid in-app currency, to add extra Hype to a video and push its visibility, available to YouTube Partner Program creators with between 500 and 500,000 subscribers in the United States, Canada, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Poland, Spain, Turkey and the United Kingdom. The same update removed the previous cap on how much Hype a viewer could give during a livestream. Separately, YouTube is testing personalised brand-partnership shelves inside Studio's shopping hub for affiliate creators, surfacing product recommendations based on a channel's own content history and estimated commission rates.

Why it mattersA boost mechanic paid for by fans rather than bought from an ad budget is a small structural bet that audience loyalty, not reach, is what actually grows a mid-size channel, and Italy gets to test it from day one.

The historical bridge

Chicago, 1936-1950

Every time attention moves somewhere unmeasured, someone builds a machine to measure it before anyone agrees on the rules

In early 1936, Arthur C. Nielsen heard MIT engineer Robert Elder describe a device he called the "Audimeter," a mechanical box wired to a radio that recorded, on a slowly rolling paper tape, every twist of the dial. Nielsen bought the technology, put the first units in homes on a trial basis in 1939, and by 1942 had built the Nielsen Radio Index on a panel of 800 Audimeter-equipped households, the first time the radio industry had a single, shared number for who was actually listening, as opposed to who advertisers hoped was listening. In 1950, with television displacing radio as the medium nobody could yet measure, Nielsen retrofitted the same Audimeter hardware to track channel changes on a TV set instead of a radio dial and launched the Nielsen Television Index the same year it acquired rival ratings firm C.E. Hooper, consolidating the new TV numbers under one name before anyone else could claim the standard.

Why it still holds. The IAB's new AI-Era Attribution Blueprint and SparkToro's traffic data (The world, above) are the same move, 90 years later: attention has moved somewhere, AI answers and AI-assisted journeys this time, that nobody has a shared, trusted instrument to measure yet, so the industry is racing to build one and call it the standard before the next platform shift makes the question moot again.

Radar

  • Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEOResigned November 12 after 33 years, four days after admitting infidelity and amid a board inquiry into reports he was a foreign-intelligence target; CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO. Not a marketing story on its own, but the company whose chips sit under most of the AI stack this brief covers every issue just lost the founder who was its most recognisable brand asset.
  • Anthropic's rewritten Usage PolicyEffective November 12, adds a ban on "sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior" toward its models. Relevant here only because Priceline's Penny (issue 25) runs on Claude; worth watching whether any AI-ad assistant built on a foundation model runs into a policy line like this one.
  • Woolworths' first trans-Tasman campaignWorth a follow-up next year: does Droga5 ANZ keep one creative platform running across Australia and New Zealand, or was this a one-off.
